  He lay there on his back, his chest heaving, smelling scorched wool and the sharp tang of his own singed hair.

  The lens swept on. Smooth. Silent. Cold. The gears turned, teeth slotting into teeth with the steady, quiet crunch of oiled steel.

  Tick-click-tock.

  Above him, the light flared, flashed across the domed roof, and wheeled into the void.

  Arthur pulled himself up onto his knees. His arm was shaking, the skin of his wrist bruised deep purple where the drive-frame had pinched it against the
  guard, but the bones were whole. He picked up the broken button from the floor. He dropped it into his pocket.

  Then he picked up the horsehair brush, leaned over the rail with cold precision, and skimmed the speck of soot from the surface of the mercury. The silver
  pooled clean again, unbroken, reflecting the steady flame of the mantle like a molten mirror.

  The horn boomed again. The tower shuddered.

  Arthur looked at his pocket watch. The twenty-four minutes were up. The weight had dropped another twelve feet down the well.

  He walked to the crank, fitted the iron handle into the ratchet, and began to wind.

  One. Two. Three.

  His muscles pulled against the familiar resistance of eighty-four pounds of lead hanging in the dark. He counted each stroke aloud, his voice swallowed
  entirely by the next roar of the diaphone, his boots braced against the damp stones.

  Sixteen. Seventeen. Eighteen.

  Outside, somewhere in the pale, impenetrable milk of the fog, a three-thousand-ton iron tramp steamer might be feeling its way south from the Clyde, its
  master standing on the bridge-wing with salt in his beard, straining his ears for the grunt of a horn and his eyes for the brief, white bloom of a beam
  through the gray. That master had a wife in Greenock and three coal-trimmers down in the stokehold who had never learned to swim. They did not know Arthur
  Vance. They did not know the smell of his stale tea or the ache in his left wrist. They knew only that if the light on Eilean Dubh stopped turning for
  forty minutes, their world would end on the black teeth of the North Skerry with the roar of tearing plates and cold salt water drowning the fireboxes.

  Arthur leaned into the thirty-second turn. The ratchet clicked into its final notch. The weight was home at the ceiling of the shaft.

  He wiped the sweat from his eyes with the back of his uninjured arm, set the crank in its corner, and took his station by the circular glass, watching the
  wheel of the white light divide the dark.
